topics.title: Appendix D — Framework Integration Blueprints
topics.summary: The default companion is intentionally small enough to build with C++20, SQLite, and the Linux interfaces used by its transport. This appendix describes how to introduce common production frameworks without confusing a design blueprint with an executed integration. No gRPC server, broker cluster, TLS deployment, OpenTelemetry collector, or Kubernetes workload is started by the supplied default build.

topics.title: D.1 Replace the Transport Without Replacing the Domain
topics.summary: A gRPC adapter should translate generated request types into the same canonical domain request used by the current service. It should call the same application/store boundary and translate outcomes deliberately. The key grammar, integer range, duplicate meaning, and accepted-versus-completed distinction should not change merely because the wire format changes.

topics.title: D.2 Preserve Deadline and Cancellation Semantics
topics.summary: Use the framework’s supported deadline mechanism and document the caller’s budget. A request that expires before acceptance can fail without creating a durable obligation. A cancellation after the gateway transaction commits does not roll that transaction back. The client must retain its key to resolve an uncertain response.

topics.title: D.4 Introduce a Broker Through the Existing Outbox
topics.summary: A broker adapter can publish pending intent from the gateway outbox and let workers consume it. The transaction committing acceptance still needs to preserve the outgoing obligation. A successful network publish does not replace the local record unless the protocol defines how uncertainty is resolved.
